Learning Objectives
Develop a systematic physical examination for nonarthritic hip pain.
Understand the sensitivity and specificity of various physical examination maneuvers for
diagnosing hip pain.
Understand the relationship between the hip and the spine on physical examination.
Introduction
To optimally examine a patient with hip pain, the physician must have a solid understanding of
the possible etiologies of hip pain1-4 (Table 1).
A thoughtful and thorough routine should be followed to avoid missed hip pathology.
Both extremities should be examined and compared.

Introduction
Physical examination of the hip provides crucial information for assessing and managing
nonarthritic hip pain. The diagnosis of conditions such as femoroacetabular
impingement (FAI) without a corresponding clinical evaluation is impossible because
their definitions are based, in part, on physical examination findings.5 To best tailor the
physical examination to the patient, the physician must have a solid understanding of
the etiologies of hip pain.
The layered approach to the hip is a helpful framework to understand the multiple pain
generators that may be present in the hip from a single underlying pathology, and it can
help organize findings from the physical examination.6,7 In this framework, the hip is
divided into four layers: osseous, capsuloligamentous, myotendinous, and neurokinetic.
Pain may be from any or all of these layers as the hip adapts to a single structural
abnormality.
This lesson provides an overview of the physical examination of the hip, with an
emphasis on nonarthritic causes of hip pain. The lesson is organized by type of
examination maneuver (gait, inspection, palpation, strength/neurologic tests, and special
maneuvers). Although the flow of the physical examination can be tailored to clinician
preference, the most efficient sequence is to perform all pertinent maneuvers in one
position before moving to the next position (eg, standing, seated, supine, lateral, and
prone examinations; Video 1.

Evaluation of Gait, Posture, and Lumbar Mobility
Gait Examination
Pathologic gaits in patients with hip pain include an antalgic gait, a Trendelenburg gait,
extensor lurch, a winking gait, and short leg limp.
Femoral version abnormalities can be detected via the foot progression angle.

Gait Examination
Pathology of the hip joint often affects gait; therefore, careful observation of movement
is essential during the hip examination. Normal walking gait is well defined8-10;
(Resource 1). Careful attention should be paid to the width of the base, foot progression
angle, length of step, cadence, knee flexion angle, center of gravity, trunk shift, and
pelvic rotation. These are best assessed in a hallway in which at least three or four stride
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:44 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001067
5/36

lengths can be observed.11 Patients may be assessed via toe and heel walking because
both increase stress at the hemipelvis and may reveal subtle pain processes.
Pain is provoked in the stance phase of gait more often than in the swing phase of gait
(ie, affected patients will adopt an antalgic gait to minimize time in the stance phase).
Weakness of the gluteus medius will force the pelvis to drop on the contralateral hip,
and the patient will lurch toward the involved hip to place the center of gravity over the
hip (ie, Trendelenburg gait or abductor lurch). Conversely, weakness of the gluteus
maximus will cause the patient to lurch the trunk posteriorly during gait to maintain hip
extension at heel strike (ie, maximus or extensor lurch). A pelvic winking gait is defined
by excessive rotation toward the affected hip, designed to achieve terminal hip
extension via extension and rotation of the lumbar spine. This gait is associated with
intra-articular hip pathology and hip flexion contractures and may occur in combination
with increased lumbar lordosis or a forward-stooping posture.12 Finally, a short leg limp
may suggest a true limb-length discrepancy or functional discrepancy caused by
tightness of the iliotibial band or the hip flexors.11
The foot progression angle describes the angle of the long axis of a patient’s foot relative
to an imaginary straight line in the patient’s path while walking. The angle, which also
may be affected by dynamic torsion forces,13 is the total effect of a patient’s structural
alignment and may indicate version abnormalities contributing to hip pathology. In-
toeing represents a negative angular value, whereas out-toeing represents a positive
angular value. Although the cause of an abnormal foot progression may be
multifactorial, femoral version often plays a role; excess femoral anteversion contributes
to in-toeing, and excess femoral retroversion contributes to out-toeing. If the foot
progression angle is normal but clear genu valgum is observed during gait or stance, the
patient may have miserable malalignment (increased femoral anteversion and
compensatory increased external tibial torsion).14
Posture and Lumbar Mobility
Pelvic obliquity
Trendelenburg test
SEND FEEDBACK

6/36

Single-leg stance phase test
Increased lordosis and increased anterior pelvic tilt may be observed in patients with hip pain.
This is the result of weakness of the anterior abdominal muscles and/or tightness of the hip
flexors. For example, patients with tight hip flexors may compensate with increased lumbar
lordosis to maintain gaze forward rather than toward the ground.
The standing spine examination includes the Adam forward bend test, modified Shober test,
and Stork test.

Posture and Lumbar Mobility
The hip joint contributes to and relies on the lumbopelvic complex, resulting in an
overlap of pathology in the hip and lumbar spine.15 Therefore, upright posture and
lumbar mobility must be assessed as part of the hip examination.
During this assessment, the physician sits in front of or behind the standing patient and
feels the iliac crests to evaluate for pelvic obliquity,16 which may be a sign of true leg-
length discrepancy, hip contracture, or structural scoliosis. In patients with a leg-length
discrepancy, the Coleman block test may be used to level the pelvis, with a suspected
true or apparent leg-length discrepancy later confirmed in the supine position
Abductor weakness may occur secondary to hip pathology, such as a gluteus medius
tendinopathy or tear, or secondary to coxa vara, or it may be a sign of lumbar
radiculopathy (L4 through S1). Abductor weakness can be assessed via the
Trendelenburg test (sensitivity, 46% to 75%; specificity, 83% to 97%).17 For this test, the
examiner is seated behind the patient and palpates both greater trochanters as they
relate to the posterior superior iliac spine, which should be level. The patient is then
asked to stand on one leg. The gluteus medius of the stance leg should contract to
elevate the pelvis on the unsupported side. The test is positive if the pelvis on the
unsupported side drops down, indicating weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the
stance side (Figure 1). The single-leg stance phase test is similar to the Trendelenburg
test but emphasizes the proprioception of the abductors and core musculature. In this
test, the patient stands with the feet shoulder width apart and lifts the unaffected leg for

9/3/26, 5:44 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001067
7/36

a 6-second hold. Similar to the Trendelenburg test, the test is positive if a pelvic shift or
drop occurs.11
Figure 1 Photograph shows patient positioning for the Trendelenburg test. The patient
stands with one leg lifted. The examination is positive if the pelvis drops toward the lifted
leg, indicating weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus of the weight-bearing limb.
Palpation of the greater trochanters and the iliac crest or the posterior superior iliac
spine may aid in detection of subtle ipsilateral pelvic drop. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen,
MD, Seattle, WA.)
Overall posture and lumbopelvic mechanics may be evaluated via a standing spine
examination. In the sagittal plane, slight lordosis should be observed in the spine. Loss
of lordosis may indicate paravertebral muscle spasm. In patients with hip pain, increased
lordosis and increased anterior pelvic tilt may be observed because of weakness of the
anterior abdominal muscles and/or tightness of the hip flexors.18 Patients with tight hip
flexors may compensate with increased lumbar lordosis to maintain gaze forward rather
than toward the ground (Figure 2).

Scoliosis may be assessed by palpating along the entire spine, and thoracic imbalances
may be observed with the Adams forward bend test. This maneuver can be combined
with an assessment of overall lumbar flexion, such as the modified Schober test.19
Lumbar extension also is assessed for motion and pain. The Stork test may be
performed to evaluate for spondylolysis. During this test, the patient stands on one leg
with the unsupported leg resting on the contralateral knee. The patient is then asked to
lean back; a positive test elicits lumbar pain with extension.

C sign
Leg-length discrepancy
Intra-articular pain related to FAI or arthritis does not typically cause areas of tenderness
unless it occurs in combination with iliopsoas tendonitis, greater trochanteric pain syndrome,
athletic pubalgia, or other pathology
Areas of palpation may include the adductor longus origin, rectus abdominis insertion, pubic
symphysis/tubercle, inguinal ring, anterolateral joint line (rectus/iliopsoas), anterior superior
iliac spine, greater trochanter, sacroiliac joints, coccyx, ischial tuberosity, iliac crest, and
piriformis.

Inspection and Palpation of the Hip
Inspection and palpation play an important role in the hip examination. During the
patient history, the examiner should note the locations of patient-reported pain and
provoking factors. For example, intra-articular processes, such as FAI, typically cause
pain in the anterior groin; affected patients may cup their hip girdle at the level of the
greater trochanter, with their fingers pointing toward the groin, which is known as the C
sign (Figure 3). Patients with FAI or other intra-articular pathology also may prefer to
lean back in the examination chair with the affected hip slightly extended because hip
flexion causes pain

Figure 3 Photograph shows the C sign. Patients with intra-articular pathology, such as
femoroacetabular impingement syndrome, often localize pain by cupping the thumb and
index finger in the shape of the letter C at the hip joint. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD,
Seattle, WA.)
The hip girdle should be examined for surgical scars, atrophy, erythema, ecchymosis, or
swelling. In patients with acute muscle trauma, such as a proximal hamstring rupture,
adductor strain, or rectus avulsion, ecchymosis and swelling may be observed along the
thigh. Leg lengths in the supine position should be assessed and any discrepancy
evaluated as apparent or true.18 In patients with more severe pathology, flexion or
rotational contractures of the hip also may be noted. Ipsilateral decrease in thigh
circumference may indicate chronic conditions and muscle atrophy.20
Depending on the structure to be assessed, palpation may be performed with the
patient in the supine, lateral, or prone positions. Areas of palpation include the adductor
longus origin, rectus abdominis insertion, pubic symphysis/tubercle, inguinal ring,
anterolateral joint line (rectus/iliopsoas), anterior superior iliac spine, greater trochanter,
sacroiliac joints, coccyx, ischial tuberosity, iliac crest, and piriformis (Resource 2). The

Range of Motion Tests
Passive range of motion (ROM) should be compared bilaterally and can be assessed in the
supine, seated, and/or prone positions.
ROM of the hip includes assessment of
Internal rotation
External rotation
Flexion
Extension
Abduction
Adduction

Range of Motion Tests
Passive ROM assessment is critical for assessing osseous and ligamentous functions in
the hip. Passive ROM should be compared bilaterally and can be performed in the
supine, seated, and prone positions. In each position, ensure no additional motion from
pelvis rotation or lumbar flexion occurs because these can exaggerate hip ROM. The
limit of ROM is indicated by the initial firm end point or by patient pain. Pushing past this
end point may cause compensatory motion from the pelvis or spine and result in an
inaccurate measurement. Mean reported values for ROM of the adult hip are listed in
Table 2;18,23,24 and vary depending on patient position and measurement technique.

In the supine or seated position, internal and external rotation are assessed with the hip
and knee flexed to 90° (Figure 5). The advantage of the seated position is that the
ischium is square to the examination table, which provides stability for accurate
measurement of rotation.11 In the prone position, internal and external rotation are
assessed with the hip in neutral (Figure 6). A difference in rotation may be noted with
the hip in flexion versus extension; in the flexed position, the medial and lateral arms of
the iliofemoral ligament are released and allow for more ligamentous rotation. The
prone position also can be used to estimate femoral anteversion (Craig test).

In the supine position, hip flexion is assessed with the knee in flexion, stopping before
the pelvis lifts off the examination table. Placing a hand under the patient’s lumbar spine
will ensure that the spine is flat and that motion is from the hip (Figure 7). If direct
flexion of the hip provokes groin pain, extra-articular subspine (anterior inferior iliac
spine) impingement may be present.25 With the hip in flexion, the contralateral hip can
be examined for extension. If the patient cannot extend the contralateral hip straight on
the examination table with a flat back, a flexion contracture is present (Thomas test). As
the hip is passively returning from flexion to extension, audible pops or other
mechanical noises occur. These sounds may be indicative of a snapping iliopsoas tendon
or labral pathology (coxa saltans interna or internal snapping).26,27 Passive hip
abduction and adduction also can be assessed in the supine position to evaluate for
adductor injury (pain or guarding with passive abduction) or osteoarthritis (loss of
adduction or abduction).2,28,29
Figure 7 Photograph shows assessment of hip flexion with the patient in the supine
position. Placing a hand under the back ensures that the spine is flat during evaluation,
specifying motion from the hip joint. The contralateral hip can be simultaneously
evaluated for flexion contracture. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)

Causes of Abnormal Hip Motion
Increased femoral anteversion or retroversion
Decreased internal rotation may be one of the first signs of intra-articular disease, such as FAI
(sensitivity, 70% to 98%; specificity, 8% to 44%) or osteoarthritis.
Increased hip mobility may be a sign of instability of the hip and should prompt an
examination for global hypermobility.

Causes of Abnormal Hip Motion
Excessive femoral version or torsion may affect ROM. Normal adult femoral anteversion
is approximately 15°18 With increased anteversion, hip internal rotation is increased and
external rotation is decreased relative to mean values. The opposite is true in femoral
retroversion. Decreased internal rotation may be one of the first signs of intra-articular
disease, such as FAI (sensitivity, 70% to 98%; specificity, 8% to 44%), osteoarthritis,
adhesive capsulitis, and effusion.3,30,31 Obligate external rotation may be observed
during flexion in hips that have progressed toward osteoarthritis or in younger patients
with slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Increased hip mobility may be a sign of instability
of the hip, which may result from dysplasia, connective tissue disorders, trauma, prior
surgery, or other causes.32 If hypermobility is a concern, the examiner should perform a
global hypermobility examination, such as the Beighton score.33
Neurologic Examination and Strength Tests
Abnormal sensation about the hip joint may indicate local nerve entrapment.
The hip may be weak because of pain or injury rather than a neurologic etiology. Resistance
testing of the adductors, abductors, extensors, and flexors is a routine component of the hip
examination.
A positive resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield test) suggests intra-articular or iliopsoas
pathology. Seated resisted hip flexion is more specific for iliopsoas pathology than intra-
articular pathology.


Neurologic Examination and Strength Tests
Given the frequent overlap of lumbar and hip pathology, a thorough lower extremity
neurologic evaluation should be included in every hip examination (Resource 3 and
Resource 4). Sensation to light touch should be evaluated throughout the lower
extremity. Abnormal sensation about the hip joint may indicate local nerve entrapment.
For example, a characteristic sign of meralgia paresthetica is decreased sensation or
paresthesia in the distribution of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve because of
entrapment as the nerve travels beneath the inguinal ligament.3 Injuries such as
proximal hamstring ruptures may result in neurapraxia of the sciatic nerve or the
posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh.
Strength testing, graded on a traditional five-point scale, is a routine component of the
hip examination. The adductors, abductors, extensors, and flexors should be assessed
by applying a force to the limb and instructing the patient to resist the force. The hip
may be weak because of pain or injury rather than neurologic etiology. If a muscle or
tendon has been injured, strength tests may elicit pain without weakness in the specific
group tested.
The strength of hip adduction or abduction can be assessed in a supine, seated, or
lateral position. Pain or weakness on adductor testing may indicate tendinopathy or a
tear of the adductors or may be a sign of athletic pubalgia because of the pull of the
adductor longus on the aponeurotic plate.2,29 Posterolateral pain or weakness on
resisted hip abduction is a sign of greater trochanteric pain syndrome or gluteus medius
tendinopathy/tear. Assessment of hip abduction with the knee flexed releases the
iliotibial band and allows for more specific evaluation of the gluteus medius.11 In
patients with a hamstring tear, tendonitis, or ischial bursitis, hamstring strength should
be assessed with isolated knee flexion and isolated hip extension.
Resisted hip flexion may be assessed in the supine or seated position. The supine
resisted straight leg raise, or the Stinchfield test, is a sensitive but nonspecific test for
intra-articular and extra-articular pathology. The patient is asked to perform a straight
leg raise at 30° to 45° and resist downward pressure on the thigh (Figure 8). This places

stress on the iliopsoas, which may then cause pressure on the anterolateral labrum. The
test is positive if pain or weakness is elicited, indicating intra-articular pathology or hip
flexor pathology.11
Figure 8 Photograph shows the Stinchfield test for assessing iliopsoas and intra-articular
pain. The patient performs a straight leg raise to 30° to 45° while resisting downward
pressure on the thigh. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)
Seated resisted hip flexion is a more specific test for evaluation of the iliopsoas. The
patient is seated at the edge of the examination table and asked to flex the hip up off the
examination table and resist downward pressure (Figure 9). The patient should be asked
to avoid leaning back and engaging the abdominal muscles. This position moves the
iliopsoas away from the anterolateral labrum and, therefore, more specifically targets
the iliopsoas (and the secondary flexor, the rectus femoris) rather than the joint.

Provocative Tests/Special Tests
Provocative tests assess for impingement, flexor tendonitis, capsular laxity, sports hernia, and
other diagnoses.
Common tests are described with the patient in the supine position followed by the seated
and prone positions.
Results on the symptomatic side always should be compared with those on the contralateral
side.
Most of these tests are associated with good sensitivity but poor specificity; therefore, none
stands alone in the diagnosis of hip pathology.17

Logroll Test

Logroll Test
The logroll test, or the passive supine rotation test, is specific for hip pain. As the relaxed
hip is rolled back and forth with the patient in the supine position, only the femoral head
is moved in relation to the acetabulum and capsule. No major excursion or stress is
placed on the muscles or nerves. A positive test suggests intra-articular inflammation (ie,
synovitis, infection, fracture) and a hip that will not tolerate extensive physical
examination maneuvers.3,20
FADIR Test

FADIR Test
The FADIR test, or the anterior impingement test, may be conducted with the patient in
the supine or lateral position. The hip joint is brought into at least 90° of flexion in
combination with adduction and internal rotation (Figure 10). If pain is provoked in the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:44 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001067
21/36

groin, the test is positive. With this test, the anterolateral femoral head-neck junction is
brought into contact with the anterosuperior acetabular rim. This impinges the labrum
and cartilage in this area and, therefore, causes pain if the structures are torn or
unstable. Although the FADIR test is 59% to 100% sensitive for the diagnosis of FAI, it is
associated with poor specificity for the diagnosis of FAI (2% to 75%) because the test will
be uncomfortable in any patient with an irritated hip.31
Figure 10 Photograph shows the flexion, adduction, and internal rotation (FADIR) test,
which places the hip in a position of impingement. The test is positive if it causes groin
pain. The test is associated with a high sensitivity but a low specificity for the diagnosis of
femoroacetabular impingement. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)

The FABER test, or Patrick test, is another test used to evaluate FAI. With the patient in
the supine position, the lower extremity is placed in a figure-of-4 position, with the foot
resting on the contralateral knee (Figure 11). The knee is then lowered as far as possible,
using the width of the examiner’s fist to standardize the measurement (ie, a FABER test
of 2 signifies that two fists fit under the knee). The test is positive if it provokes pain in
the groin. The test also may cause pain posterolaterally, indicating abductor or
trochanteric pathology, or may provoke pain in a symptomatic sacroiliac joint. The FABER
test is associated with a sensitivity of 42% to 60% and a specificity of 18% to 75% for the
diagnosis of FAI.31
Figure 11 Photograph shows the flexion, abduction, and external rotation (FABER) test,
which stresses the hip joint, abductors, and sacroiliac joint. The location of pain (anterior,
posterolateral, posterior) may indicate the underlying pathology. (Courtesy of Mia S.
Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)


Dynamic Tests
The hip can be assessed for impingement and labral tears via various dynamic tests. The
Scour test, or dynamic labral stress test (sensitivity 50%, specificity 29%), is performed
with the patient in the supine position and the hip in at least 90° of flexion and slight
abduction.31 The hip is then axially compressed via internal and external rotation at
multiple degrees of hip abduction. Groin pain and/or clicking is considered a positive
test.34 Similarly, with the McCarthy hip extension test, the affected hip is taken from
flexion into extension as it is rolled in arcs of internal and external rotation. The test is
positive if hip extension causes anterior pain or a pop.
The DEXRIT test and the DIRIT test differ from the McCarthy test in that the contralateral
hip is held in flexion by the patient, which may eliminate the effect of lumbar lordosis on
hip motion on the affected side. The affected hip is then brought through a wide arc of
abduction and external rotation (DEXRIT) followed by adduction and internal rotation
(DIRIT)11
Foveal Distraction Test

Foveal Distraction Test
The foveal distraction test is another maneuver for assessing intra-articular pathology.
During this test, the limb is moved into 30° of abduction, and passive axial traction is
applied. If this relieves hip pain, the test is positive.3

In the Thomas test, the patient is brought to the edge of the examination table and holds
both knees to the chest in a supine position. The affected leg is actively lowered into
extension toward the examination table. If the thigh cannot reach the examination table,
the test is positive for a hip flexor contraction (psoas, rectus femoris, and/or iliotibial
band; Figure 12).
Figure 12 Photographs show the Thomas test. The maneuver is performed at the edge
of the examination table with both hips initially flexed. A, One limb is slowly brought into
extension while the other limb is held in flexion. B, The test is positive for hip flexor
contraction if the thigh cannot reach a horizontal position. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen,
MD, Seattle, WA.)
PRI Test

PRI Test
The PRI test is performed with the patient in the supine position and the limb abducted,
extended off the examination table, and externally rotated. To limit lumbar lordosis
during this maneuver, the patient alternatively may be positioned at the end of the
examination table with the contralateral limb held to the chest11 (Figure 13). The test is
positive if buttock pain is elicited as the femoral head contacts the posterior acetabular
rim and cartilage. This finding is common in patients with global acetabular coverage,
such as coxa profunda or protrusio, or unstable posterior os acetabuli.35 A positive test

(particularly the quadratus femoris); however, passive adduction with extension should

Figure 13 Photograph shows the posterior rim impingement (PRI) test, which is
performed with the hip abducted and extended and the knee in flexion. The test is
positive if it elicits posterior (buttock) pain as the hip is externally rotated, which presses
the femoral head on the posterior acetabular rim. This test can be slightly modified as
the hyperextension external rotation (HEER) or anterior apprehension test by pressing
down on the distal thigh while externally rotating the hip, which stresses the anterior
capsule (not pictured). In the HEER test, anterior pain or guarding indicates a positive
test result. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)

The HEER test, or the anterior apprehension test, measures capsular laxity using patient
positioning similar to that for the PRI test (Figure 13). The patient is placed in the supine
position at the end of the examination table with the buttocks at the edge of the
examination table. The knee is held to the chest while the examiner brings the other
extremity into hyperextension and external rotation; the examiner then presses down
on the thigh while externally rotating the hip, stressing the anterior capsule and labrum.
The test is positive if it produces anterior pain or guarding. The test has is associated
with a sensitivity of 71% and a specificity of 85% for the diagnosis of hip instability.32
Dial Test

Dial Test
The dial test also assesses anterior capsular laxity. With the patient in the supine
position and legs extended, both feet are passively rolled into maximum internal
rotation. The examiner then releases the feet. The test is positive if the limb externally
rotates beyond 45° with no rebound to the neutral position.26,34
Internal Snapping

Internal Snapping
Internal snapping can be produced voluntarily with active motion and is a common
incidental finding during a hip physical examination; however, it occasionally causes
pain. Internal snapping can be provoked by moving the hip from flexion, abduction, and
external rotation to extension, adduction, and internal rotation; an audible pop is then
heard.4 This occurs as the iliopsoas tendon slides over the anterior hip capsule and the
pectineal eminence.


Resisted Sit-up Test
If athletic pubalgia is suspected, a sit-up test can be performed to confirm the diagnosis.
For this test, the patient is placed in the supine position with the hips and knees flexed.
The patient then attempts to sit up while the examiner stabilizes the contralateral pelvis
and pushes on the ipsilateral shoulder. The test is positive if pain is present at the lateral
edge of the distal rectus abdominis.2,6
Passive Straight Leg Raise

Passive Straight Leg Raise
If lumbar pathology is suspected, the passive straight leg raise may reveal lumbar nerve
root irritation. During this test, the affected leg is raised with the knee extended. The test
is positive if radicular pain is provoked from 30° to 60° of flexion. The contralateral
straight leg raise test is positive if the affected leg experiences radicular symptoms as the
opposite leg is raised from 30° to 60° of flexion.37

The Ober test assesses contracture of the iliotibial band and the abductors. With the
patient in the lateral position, the knee is flexed to 90° while the examiner holds the limb
distal to the knee. The hip is then passively brought into maximal extension while the
limb is lowered (adducted). The test is positive if the knee is unable to adduct past
midline (Figure 14).
Variations of the Ober test are the three passive adduction tests, whereby the hip is
passively adducted in three different positions (extension with knee extended, neutral
with knee flexed, and flexion with knee extended and the shoulders rolled back on the
table). These three positions measure contracture of the tensor fascia lata, gluteus
medius, and gluteus maximus, respectively, if the hip is unable to passively adduct past
the midline of the body.11
Figure 14 Photograph shows the Ober test, in which the limb is brought into extension
and abduction and slowly lowered with the knee flexed to 90°. The test is positive if the
knee cannot be adducted past midline. (Courtesy of Mia S. Hagen, MD, Seattle, WA.)


Bicycle Test
During the bicycle test, the patient re-creates the motion of peddling a bicycle (ie, active
flexion and extension of the hip) in the lateral position. The test is positive for external
snapping if audible snapping or clunking is noted as the iliotibial band and tensor fascia
lata slide over the greater trochanter. This snapping often is visible. Similar to internal
snapping, external snapping can be re-created voluntarily.
Pubic Symphysis Stress Test

Pubic Symphysis Stress Test
Also known as the lateral compression test, the pubic symphysis stress test is performed
by placing downward pressure on the greater trochanter or the iliac crest with the
patient in the lateral decubitus position. The test is positive if the patient experiences
discomfort. Pain at the pubic symphysis may indicate osteitis pubis, whereas pain
posteriorly may indicate sacroiliac joint dysfunction.2,38
Piriformis Tests

Piriformis Tests
True sciatic nerve entrapment at the level of the piriformis muscle (ie, piriformis
syndrome) is rare and often difficult to diagnose. Burning or cramping in the buttock or
the posterior thigh may be a sign of piriformis syndrome. Additional piriformis tests may
help confirm the diagnosis. The active piriformis test is performed with the patient in the
lateral position, with the affected side up, and the heel pushing into the table (Figure 15,
A). The patient then actively abducts the leg with external rotation against resistance as
the examiner palpates the piriformis. Posterior pain or weakness with this maneuver
indicates a positive test. The seated piriformis stretch test (Figure 15, B) can provide
